newsitem.title: UK: UK highly unlikely to join first wave of EMU-Blair.
newsitem.headline: UK highly unlikely to join first wave of EMU-Blair.

text.p: Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair said on Thursday that it was "highly unlikely" that Britain would join a European single currency on January 1, 1999.

Speaking at a school in Redditch, central England, Blair said there were advantages in principle to a single currency but added: "It has got to be economically right for Britain and it should not be politically driven."
"It is a very big step and unless the economies fit together properly, it could do very real damage," said Blair, campaigning ahead of a May 1 election his party is favourite to win.
Labour's position on the single currency is virtually indistinguishable from that of the ruling Conservatives. Both have promised a national referendum on joining European Monetary Union (EMU).

Blair said Labour would take a decision on EMU in the country's economic interests but whatever that decision was, it would be dangerous for Britain to pull out of negotiations on the form the single currency would take.
"It is very important that we keep our place at the negotiating table," Blair said.
"I think it is highly unlikely we would be in the first wave but if we are, there would be a referendum on it."

Challenged by a school pupil about whether Labour's plan for a national minimum wage would cost jobs, Blair said that if the U.S. experience was anything to go by, it need not boost the unemployment level.
He said Labour would have to "set it at the right level for the economy and then you can raise it when you can".
